title: Critical Theory
summary: Critical theory's Frankfurt School roots, its goal of emancipation, its Gramscian idea of hegemony, Robert Cox, and its core assumptions.

lesson.title: Theory for emancipation, not just criticism
lesson.hook: Most students think 'critical theory' means a theory that criticises other theories. It does not. The word 'critical' here is about freeing people, and that difference wins marks.

slides.heading: What 'critical' really means
slides.body:
**Critical theory** entered International Relations in the **mid-1980s**. Its name is misleading. It is not called critical because it attacks realism or liberalism (although it does).

It is called critical because its central concern is **human emancipation**: how theory can help free the oppressed people of the world. A critical theorist asks not only 'how does the world work?' but 'how can it be changed so fewer people are dominated?'

slides.heading: Born in Frankfurt
slides.body:
The roots lie in the **Institute of Social Research** in Frankfurt, Germany, founded in **1923** and known as the **Frankfurt School**. The term 'critical theory' was formally coined in **1937**, in Max Horkheimer's essay contrasting traditional and critical theory.

The School studied why ordinary people supported **fascism**, linking it to the **authoritarian personality**, and asked how science and technology could weaken people's capacity for **critical reason**.

terms.meaning: Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse, Benjamin, Pollock, Lowenthal and Fromm.
Leads the second generation from the 1970s; opened dialogue between continental and analytic philosophy and made the School global.
American philosopher, contemporary of Habermas, who spread critical theory in US universities.
Brought Gramscian critical theory into International Relations.
Major critical IR theorist; wrote Beyond Realism and Marxism (1989).

slides.question: Critical theory is so named mainly because it:
options: Criticises every rival perspective in IR
Is concerned with using theory for human emancipation
Was formed to criticise the League of Nations
slides.why: The defining concern is emancipation of the oppressed. Criticising rivals is a side effect, not the reason for the name, and it actually draws on Marxism.

slides.heading: Hegemony: a different meaning
slides.body:
**Hegemony** is central to critical theory, but not in the realist sense. Realists use it for the **overwhelming power of one state** or group of states, like the USA after the Cold War.

Critical theorists, following the Italian Marxist **Antonio Gramsci**, read hegemony through **class relations**. A class is hegemonic when its rule is **accepted as legitimate**, because it has built institutions and made concessions so that others go along willingly. Consent, not just force, is the point.

slides.heading: The historic bloc
slides.body:
When a class has legitimised its dominance through institutions and concessions, **and** also controls the formal political structure of the state, it forms a **historic bloc**.

Think of it as a ruling alliance that has won both the government and the minds of the people. Its power feels normal, even natural, which is exactly why it is hard to challenge.

slides.heading: Why nobody riots
slides.story: In a hostel at UI, Musa asks why workers on poor wages rarely protest. Chiamaka answers that the employers give small bonuses at Christmas, sponsor church harvests and own the radio station everyone listens to. Many workers now believe that hard work alone will make them rich, so they blame themselves rather than the system.
slides.takeaway: Concessions, institutions and ideas win consent: that is hegemony in the Gramscian sense, not raw force.

slides.question: A class that has made its rule seem legitimate through institutions and concessions, and also controls the formal state, constitutes a:
slides.why: That combination is what critical theorists call a historic bloc. A core state belongs to structuralist core–periphery language.

left.title: Realist hegemony
points: Predominant power of a state
Measured in military and economic might
Rests mainly on capability
Example: a superpower

right.title: Critical (Gramscian) hegemony
points: Dominance of a class or bloc
Rests on consent and legitimacy
Built through culture, ideas, institutions
Outcome of class struggle

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: The favourite question asks how critical theory's idea of hegemony departs from the realist one. The trap is to define hegemony only as a dominant state. Another trap: saying critical theory is named for criticising other theories.
slides.sampleQuestion: Assess the departure of critical theory from realism in its interpretation of hegemony.
slides.howToAnswer: Give the realist meaning (predominant state power), then the Gramscian one (class dominance legitimised by consent through institutions and concessions), introduce the historic bloc, and note Cox's application to world order.

points: Critical theory aims at human emancipation, not just criticising rivals.
It began with the Frankfurt School (1923); the term dates from 1937.
Habermas led the second generation; Bernstein spread it in America.
Gramscian hegemony is class dominance accepted through consent.
A legitimised class that also controls the state forms a historic bloc.

questions.stem: The central concern that gives critical theory its name is:
options: Attacking every rival theory of IR
questions.explanation: Critical theory is about how theory can help liberate the oppressed. It is a common error to think the name comes from criticising other perspectives.

questions.stem: Critical theory first became influential in International Relations in the:
questions.explanation: Critical theory gained influence in IR from the mid-1980s. The 1920s mark the founding of the Frankfurt School itself, not its arrival in IR.

questions.stem: The Frankfurt School, from which critical theory emerged, was established in:
questions.explanation: The Institute of Social Research was founded in Frankfurt in 1923. The year 1937 is when the term 'critical theory' was formally coined, a frequent trap.

questions.stem: Which of these was NOT a member of the first generation of Frankfurt School theorists?
questions.explanation: Habermas led the second generation from the 1970s. Adorno, Marcuse and Horkheimer were all first-generation figures.

questions.stem: Among other things, the early Frankfurt School studied the relationship between fascism and:
questions.explanation: The School examined how fascism connected to the authoritarian personality and how science and technology affected critical reason. Collective security is an idealist concern.

questions.stem: Critical theorists differ from realists in that they understand hegemony mainly in terms of:
options: The military superiority of a single state
Membership of the UN Security Council
questions.explanation: For critical theorists, hegemony is about a class whose dominance is accepted as legitimate. Military superiority of one state is the realist sense.

questions.stem: A ruling group stays in power for decades not mainly through soldiers but because most citizens accept its values as common sense. A critical theorist would call this:
questions.explanation: Rule that rests on widely accepted ideas is Gramscian hegemony. Balance of power concerns relations of capability between states, not consent within society.

questions.stem: Which philosopher, a contemporary of Habermas, helped develop critical theory in American universities?
questions.explanation: Richard Bernstein embraced the critical theory agenda and spread it in the United States. Benjamin, Fromm and Pollock were first-generation Frankfurt figures.

questions.stem: A business class funds schools, media and charities, grants workers small benefits, and also controls the government. In critical theory terms it has formed:
questions.explanation: Legitimised dominance through institutions and concessions, plus control of the formal state, makes a historic bloc. Periphery is a structuralist term for poor states.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Habermas – first generation of the Frankfurt School
Gramsci – realist theory of state hegemony
1923 – founding of the Institute of Social Research
questions.explanation: The Institute was founded in 1923. Habermas was second generation, 1937 is when the term was coined, and Gramsci was a Marxist, not a realist.

questions.stem: The view that hegemony rests largely on consent won through institutions and concessions, rather than on force alone, draws chiefly on the ideas of:
questions.explanation: Gramsci developed the idea of hegemony as consent-based class rule, which Cox and other critical theorists use. Morgenthau and Waltz are realists who see hegemony as state power.

questions.stem: Habermas's contribution to the Frankfurt School is particularly credited with:
options: Opening dialogue between continental and analytic traditions and globalising the School
Founding the Institute of Social Research in 1923
Creating the realist concept of national interest
questions.explanation: Habermas linked continental and analytic philosophy and carried the School's influence beyond Germany. 'Historic bloc' comes from Gramsci, and national interest is a realist concept.

questions.stem: Consider: I. Critical theory is so named because it criticises realism. II. The term was formally coined in 1937. III. Habermas led the second generation. IV. Critical theorists define hegemony solely as a state's military dominance. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: The name comes from the goal of emancipation, not criticism (I false), and critical theorists read hegemony through class and consent (IV false). II and III are correct.

questions.stem: A realist and a critical theorist both call the United States 'hegemonic' after 1991. The most accurate account of their difference is that:
options: Both mean exactly the same thing by the word
The realist stresses predominant capability; the critical theorist stresses a consent-based order backed by class forces
The realist stresses consent; the critical theorist stresses only military force
Neither theory uses the concept of hegemony
questions.explanation: Realists see hegemony as overwhelming state power, while critical theorists see an order legitimised by consent and tied to class forces. The third option reverses the two views.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why critical theorists say a historic bloc is hard to overthrow?
options: It controls the state and also commands consent, so its rule feels natural
It has the largest army in the international system
International law forbids challenges to it
It depends entirely on foreign aid
questions.explanation: A historic bloc combines control of the state with legitimacy won through institutions, concessions and ideas, so people accept it as normal. Military size is the realist measure of power.

lesson.title: Robert Cox and the five assumptions
lesson.hook: Marxists have been predicting the collapse of capitalism for more than 150 years, yet it keeps surviving. Robert Cox thought he knew why, and his answer was about ideas, not guns.

slides.heading: Robert Cox brings hegemony to world order
slides.body:
**Robert Cox** applied the idea of hegemony to the dominance of major states and to the **international economy**. In **Production, Power and World Order** (1987) he set out a theory of how **hegemonic world orders** have risen and changed in the modern era.

Cox gives **states**, especially **hegemonic states**, a bigger role than traditional Marxists did. Allied with capitalist forces, these states build a global framework in which capitalism can spread and become the dominant mode of production.

slides.heading: The original element: ideas
slides.body:
What is new in Cox, borrowed from **Gramsci**, is the key role of **ideology**. A world order is only stable and legitimate if it rests on **consensual ideas** widely accepted by other states and by **civil society**.

So the hegemonic bloc is not just a deal between political and economic power. It also pulls in parts of civil society: universities, media, churches, NGOs. This wider hegemony explains why capitalism has outlived Marxist predictions of its early collapse.

slides.question: According to Cox, the resilience of the capitalist order against predictions of collapse is best explained by:
options: The anarchic nature of the state system
A hegemony that includes consensual ideas and civil society
Pure military force by the hegemon
slides.why: Cox's extended hegemony rests on widely accepted ideas and draws in civil society, which makes the order durable. Pure force is exactly what Gramscian hegemony goes beyond.

slides.heading: Theory is always for someone
slides.body:
In a famous 1981 article, Cox wrote that **theory is always for someone and for some purpose**. He contrasted **problem-solving theory**, which takes the existing order as given and tries to make it run smoothly, with **critical theory**, which asks how that order came about and how it might be changed.

On this view, realism is problem-solving theory: useful, but it quietly protects the status quo.

slides.heading: How critical theory departs from Marxism

left.title: Traditional Marxism
points: Rigid link: economy decides society
Class is the main inequality
Capitalism must be overthrown
Little role for states

right.title: Critical theory
points: Society and state have some autonomy
Also nationality, ethnicity, race, gender
Change possible, e.g. through democracy
Hegemonic states matter (Cox)

slides.heading: Openings inside an unjust system
slides.body:
Critical theorists still see capitalism as **exploitative and oppressive**. But they believe it also creates **openings for social change** that oppositional groups can use, for instance through the **democratic process**.

They widen the idea of inequality beyond class to include **nationality, ethnic origin, race and gender**. A poor woman from a minority group may face several layers of exclusion at once.

slides.heading: #EndSARS and knowledge as power
slides.story: In October 2020, young Nigerians organised the #EndSARS protests against police brutality. Many had learned on social media how widespread the abuse was and how other countries had reformed their police. Understanding the pattern turned private fear into public action, and the government announced that the SARS unit was dissolved.
slides.takeaway: Critical theory holds that knowledge is power: understanding how you are oppressed makes action to change it possible.

slides.question: Which of these is a point on which critical theory departs from traditional Marxism?
options: It denies that capitalism is exploitative
It accepts a rigid determination of society by the economy
It recognises inequalities of race, gender and ethnicity as well as class
It sees no possibility of change within capitalism
slides.why: Critical theory widens inequality beyond class. It still calls capitalism exploitative, rejects rigid economic determinism and sees openings for change.

steps.title: Capitalist forces
steps.detail: Understand the world through the economic and social forces of capitalism, now international in reach.

steps.title: Functions of states
steps.detail: States and institutions are understood by how they support global capitalism.

steps.title: Culture and ideology
steps.detail: They support or challenge the order; hegemony legitimises capitalist rule.

steps.title: Struggle of social forces
steps.detail: Some groups defend the status quo, others fight to change it.

steps.title: Emancipation
steps.detail: Political action can change structures and free people.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'differentiate critical theory from Marxism' and 'examine two assumptions'. Students lose marks by saying critical theory rejects Marxism completely, or by forgetting Cox's emphasis on ideas and civil society. Name Cox's 1987 book; it impresses examiners.
slides.sampleQuestion: Differentiate between critical theory and Marxism, and explain how Robert Cox accounts for the survival of capitalism.
slides.howToAnswer: List the departures (autonomy of state and society, wider inequalities, openings for change, role of hegemonic states), then explain Cox's Gramscian hegemony built on consensual ideas and civil society.

points: Cox (1987) traced how hegemonic world orders form and change.
His key addition: consensual ideas and civil society stabilise hegemony.
Theory is always for someone and some purpose: problem-solving versus critical.
Critical theory rejects rigid economic determinism and widens inequality beyond class.
Knowledge is power; political action can bring emancipation.

questions.stem: Robert Cox's major work on hegemonic world orders is titled:
questions.explanation: Cox wrote Production, Power and World Order (1987). Politics Among Nations is Morgenthau's, Theory of International Politics is Waltz's, and Beyond Realism and Marxism is Linklater's.

questions.stem: Critical theory holds that 'knowledge is power'. In this context the phrase means that:
options: Understanding how one is oppressed makes it possible to act against it
questions.explanation: For critical theory, awareness of the ways one is oppressed is the first step to changing oppressive forces. It is not about military or intelligence advantage.

questions.stem: Critical theorists see culture and ideology as forces that:
options: Have no effect on international relations
Can either support or challenge the existing order
questions.explanation: Culture and ideology can uphold or resist the international social order. Saying they always oppose capitalism ignores their role in sustaining hegemony.

questions.stem: Cox's work is considered original mainly because of the key role it gives to:
questions.explanation: Inspired by Gramsci, Cox stresses that a hegemonic order must rest on widely accepted ideas. Human nature is the classical realist starting point.

questions.stem: Compared with traditional Marxists, Cox gives a greater role to:
questions.explanation: Cox attributes a bigger role to states, especially hegemonic ones, which ally with capitalist forces to spread capitalism. Traditional Marxists focused mainly on class.

questions.stem: Besides class, critical theorists identify all of the following as sources of inequality and exclusion EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Critical theory widens inequality to nationality, ethnicity, race and gender. UN membership is not one of the social inequalities it names.

questions.stem: Activists in a country with an unjust economic system win reforms by voting a new party into power. Critical theory would see this as:
options: Impossible, since capitalism allows no change
An example of capitalism producing openings that oppositional groups can use
questions.explanation: Critical theory holds that capitalism, though oppressive, creates opportunities for change such as the democratic process. It does not conclude that capitalism is fair.

questions.stem: A scholar asks how the current world order came into being and whose interests it serves, instead of how to make it run more smoothly. In Cox's terms, this scholar is doing:
questions.explanation: Cox's critical theory questions the origins of the order and how it could change. Problem-solving theory takes the order as given and tries to make it work better.

questions.stem: A critical theorist studying the World Trade Organization would primarily ask:
options: How it supports global capitalism and whose interests it serves
How many troops its members can deploy
Whether it reflects human nature's lust for power
How it preserves the balance of power
questions.explanation: A core assumption is that states and institutions are understood by the functions they perform for global capitalism. Troops and balance of power are realist concerns.

questions.stem: Which statement about critical theory and Marxism is correct?
options: Critical theory rejects the idea that capitalism is exploitative
Critical theory holds a more rigid view of economy and society than Marxism
Critical theory grants society and state a degree of autonomy
Critical theory treats class as the only form of inequality
questions.explanation: Unlike Marxism, critical theory does not see society as rigidly determined by the economy and gives state and society some autonomy. It still sees capitalism as exploitative.

questions.stem: In Cox's account, the hegemonic bloc that underpins world order rests on:
options: Political and economic forces plus key elements of civil society
The working class of the periphery
questions.explanation: Cox's extended hegemony includes civil society alongside political and economic forces. Leaving out civil society is the trap, since that is his original contribution.

questions.stem: The statement that theory is 'always for someone and for some purpose' is associated with:
questions.explanation: Cox made this argument in 1981 to show that theories serve interests. Keohane is a neo-liberal institutionalist, and Wilson is linked to idealism.

questions.stem: Consider these assumptions: I. States and institutions are understood by their functions in supporting global capitalism. II. International relations is a struggle among social forces. III. Culture and ideology are irrelevant to world order. IV. Political action can bring more emancipatory forms of existence. Which belong to critical theory?
questions.explanation: Critical theory treats culture and ideology as powerful forces, so III is false. I, II and IV are among its basic assumptions.

questions.stem: A Marxist says capitalism will soon collapse under its contradictions. A follower of Cox replies that it will probably endure. The Coxian's best reason is that:
options: Capitalism has no contradictions at all
Its hegemony is anchored in widely shared ideas and civil society, giving it legitimacy
Anarchy prevents any single class from dominating
Interdependence makes all classes equally wealthy
questions.explanation: Cox explains capitalism's resilience by its consent-based hegemony built on ideas and civil society. He does not deny contradictions; he explains why they have not toppled the system.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches the concept with its source?
options: Historic bloc – Gramsci; emancipation goal – Frankfurt School
Historic bloc – Waltz; emancipation goal – realism
Hegemony as state power – Gramsci; consent – Morgenthau
Problem-solving theory – Habermas; historic bloc – Horkheimer
questions.explanation: The historic bloc comes from Gramsci, and the goal of emancipation defines the Frankfurt School tradition. The other options attach concepts to the wrong thinkers.
